title: Lady Overseer
tagline: History's first named female doctor supervised physicians when women rarely held titles.

scenes.text: Memphis, Egypt, c. 2500 BCE. The Old Kingdom at its height. The great pyramids are already standing. And in the medical precincts of the city, a woman holds a title that should not exist — not according to anything the ancient world expects of women.

scenes.speaker: Peseshet
scenes.text: I did not seek this title. I earned it. Every woman physician under my supervision was trained here — how to read the body's signs, how to prepare medicines, how to assist in birth. Medicine does not care about the sex of the hands that practice it. Only their skill.

challenge.instruction: Peseshet's students learn from old papyri, worn and stained by damp. Restore the picture on the teaching sheet from the clues that survive.
challenge.fact: Peseshet (c. 2500–2450 BCE) is the earliest known female medical administrator in history. Her title 'Imy-r swnwt' — 'Lady Overseer of Female Physicians' — indicates she supervised a group of female medical practitioners, making her a pioneering figure in both medicine and women's leadership.

scenes.text: Peseshet's title — 'Lady Overseer of Female Physicians' — is unique in the entire corpus of ancient Egyptian texts. It implies an institution: a school or hospital where women trained as physicians under her supervision. We know of her only through an inscription in her son Akhethotep's tomb.

scenes.speaker: Young Physician
scenes.text: Lady Peseshet, the older male physicians say women should only attend to women patients — that we should not treat the men or the soldiers. Is that the law?

challenge.instruction: The young physician asks what the law allows. Peseshet points to her own title, cut in mirror letters on the wall — read it.
challenge.fact: Peseshet predates Hippocrates — the 'Father of Medicine' — by nearly 2,000 years. Her title 'Lady Overseer of Female Physicians' implies there were enough women doctors to require an administrator, suggesting female medical practice was established, not exceptional.

scenes.speaker: Peseshet
scenes.text: The patient who needs you does not care what the older physicians say. Treat the patient in front of you with every skill you have. The body's suffering is not gendered. Neither is the physician's obligation to relieve it.

challenge.instruction: The patient in front of you needs a remedy now. Measure out the dose, joining the small parts of the hekat until it is exactly right.
challenge.fact: We know of Peseshet entirely through a false door stele in her son's tomb at Giza. This was a common way for high-status women to be memorialized. The inscription preserves for 4,500 years the name of the world's first known female physician.

scenes.text: Ancient Egypt was unusually progressive regarding women in medicine. Several female physicians are attested in the historical record. Peseshet stands above them all — not merely as a practitioner, but as an administrator and educator who built an institution, trained successors, and left a legacy her son thought worth recording in stone.

challenge.instruction: Peseshet's school teaches the scribes' arithmetic along with medicine. Take the lesson beside the new pyramids of Giza and measure one by its shadow.
challenge.fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza, raised within a century of Peseshet's career, is set square to the four cardinal points to within a fraction of a degree, and its 230-metre base is level to about two centimetres.

scenes.speaker: Peseshet
scenes.text: My name will be in my son's tomb. Not as his mother — as Lady Overseer of Female Physicians. That title is the record I leave. One day someone will read it and understand: this was a place where women healed, and a woman led them. Let that be enough.

challenge.instruction: Peseshet's name will be kept in her son's tomb at Giza, among the things the dead take with them. Play senet with a student in the physicians' hall.
challenge.fact: A false door was the place in an Egyptian tomb where the living set down offerings and the spirit of the dead was believed to pass between worlds. Peseshet's own false door was set up in the tomb of her son Akhethotep.

scenes.speaker: Peseshet
scenes.text: The lesson is simple. Mahavira stands at Memphis and the Argument has begun. Bring me onto the board, put a Astronomer at my side, and let us measure Intelligence against Intelligence.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 1 · First Duel. Deploy Peseshet to Memphis, add the Astronomer, then tap Peseshet and tap Mahavira to attack. Win one attack.
challenge.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: Peseshet brings 8 Intelligence, the Astronomer adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.
